Let me start with a question. How long does it take you to pay a supplier in another country? For most of the small exporters we work with in Chile, the honest answer is too long. My name is Laura, and I lead the trade innovation team at a mid-sized bank in Santiago. We have worked with exporters for more than thirty years. Here is the problem. Inside Chile, a payment takes seconds. But when one of our small exporters sells to Brazil or to the United States, they can wait up to twelve days to get paid. Twelve days is the difference between growing and borrowing. What we are really trying to solve for is that gap. We have been running a pilot in one corridor, and the same payment now takes about twelve minutes. Twelve days to twelve minutes. So that is actually what I would love to explore with someone like you. Do you have thirty minutes for a coffee tomorrow? We could compare our corridors and see if one pilot makes sense for both sides.

The most common mistake I see in a short pitch is energy. People start with all of it. The first sentence is loud and fast, and by the end they have nothing left, which is a shame, because the end is where the request is. So try it the other way round. Make your first sentence a little slower and a little lower than normal. It sounds calm, and it makes people lean in. Then let the energy build through the problem and the solution. That is where your numbers are, so let them be louder. And when you get to the invitation, let your voice go up and then come down gently at the end. That movement sounds like an open door. A flat, falling voice sounds like the end of a speech, and nobody replies to the end of a speech.
